name: Royal jelly

lead: Royal jelly is the secretion nurse bees feed to queen larvae. It is sold as a supplement and used in cosmetics, promoted for vitality, smoother skin and a younger look.

It contains protein, sugars, lipids including 10-HDA and B vitamins, and proponents credit it with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. In bees, its proteins drive queen development. The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support human health benefits, and no trial has measured appearance.

paras: It is taken as capsules, fresh or freeze-dried jelly, or blended with honey, and it also appears in creams and serums. Users take it as a daily routine over weeks, often alongside other skin supplements.

Allergic reactions from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis have been reported, with higher risk in people with allergies. It is sold as a supplement, and the FDA has acted against unsupported health claims.

angle.text: Royal jelly is taken as a supplement and used in cosmetics for smoother, younger-looking skin, based on its bee-derived nutrients and proteins. EFSA reviewed the human health claims in 2011 and found no support.

lead: Royal jelly is a milky secretion produced by the head glands of young worker honey bees (Apis mellifera) and fed to all larvae in their first days and, throughout life, to queen larvae and adult queens.[1][2] It is harvested commercially and sold as a dietary supplement and a cosmetic ingredient, and is used in apitherapy.[2]

Its composition is roughly two-thirds water, with protein (largely major royal jelly proteins), sugars and lipids including 10-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid (10-HDA), plus B vitamins such as pantothenic acid.[1][2] Proponents credit it with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and rejuvenating properties, while the European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support health benefits in humans.[2]

Allergic reactions ranging from hives to asthma and, rarely, fatal anaphylaxis have been reported.[2] No human trial of royal jelly for skin or other appearance outcomes was identified in the sources reviewed.
infobox: EFSA (2011) found evidence did not support human health claims[2]

paras: Nurse bees secrete royal jelly from the hypopharyngeal and mandibular glands; larvae destined to be queens are fed it continuously, whereas worker larvae switch to a pollen and honey mixture after about three days.[1][2] Beekeepers harvest it from queen cells around the fourth day of larval life, and a well-managed hive may yield about 500 g over a five-to-six-month season.[1][2]

Honey bee research has examined how this diet drives caste differences. Studies reported that silencing the DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3 in larvae produced queen-like development, linking royal jelly to epigenetic control, and a 2011 Nature paper proposed that a royal jelly protein, royalactin, induces queen differentiation.[3][4][5] These are findings about bees, not humans.

Reference summaries give approximate proportions of 67% water, 12.5% protein, 11% sugars, 6% fatty acids and 3.5% 10-HDA; it lacks the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.[2] The product is perishable and typically cold-stored or freeze-dried.[1][2]
Reviews of honey-bee products have summarised laboratory, animal and some human findings on antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects, noting varied study quality.[6][7][8][9]

Registered human trials focus on other conditions: hypertension, chronic kidney disease, coronary artery disease, male infertility and upper respiratory infections, most still recruiting or with no posted results in the registry entries cited.[10][11][12] No trial of royal jelly for skin, hair or body appearance was found.

Wikipedia reports that reactions range from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis, with unknown incidence and higher risk in people with other allergies.[2] The US FDA has taken action against companies making unsupported health claims, and the product is not vegan.[2]

Royal jelly is mentioned on forums in combination with other bee products for general wellness and various body-enhancement claims. Anecdotal reports of this kind have not been examined in published studies.

timeline.event: Study reports Dnmt3 silencing mimics royal jelly effect in honey bee larvae.[3]
Royalactin study published in Nature; EFSA concludes evidence does not support human health benefits.[2][5]
